interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between a strong senior engineer and a strong staff engineer, in your own words?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The clearest difference I've seen is where the impact is capped. A strong senior engineer's impact is largely capped by their own hours and skill — they can take on a hard, ambiguous project and execute it excellently, and that's genuinely valuable. A staff engineer's impact is meant to exceed what their own hours could produce, because it runs through other people, systems, or decisions that keep paying off without their continued involvement.

Concretely: I built a contract-testing framework after noticing recurring cross-service incidents traced to undetected API mismatches. Building it took about three weeks of my own time. In the year since, twelve teams adopted it — I only personally helped the first two; the other ten found it through internal docs. The incident class it targets dropped from roughly one every three weeks to two in the whole year.

That three-week investment kept returning value to teams I never spoke to, which is categorically different from a three-week project whose value stopped the moment I shipped it. A staff engineer's job, as I understand it, is finding and building more of that first kind of thing — even when it's less flashy than a big solo technical win.

**Testing:** whether you have a real, working mental model of the level distinction, backed by a concrete example, rather than a vague sense that staff just means "more senior."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Level distinction

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you set a technical direction that multiple teams ended up building against.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Over about six months, I noticed a pattern: nearly every new feature request across three product teams involved some form of asynchronous processing, and each team was building its own bespoke queue-and-worker setup, with subtly different failure-handling and retry semantics each time.

Rather than wait for this to become an official mandate from someone above me, I proposed a shared event-streaming architecture, built a reference implementation for one real use case first — not just a design doc — and made adopting it clearly the path of least resistance: better documentation, an existing on-call runbook, and pre-built failure-handling than any team would get building their own from scratch.

It wasn't adopted because I told anyone to use it. Two of the three teams adopted it voluntarily within the following two quarters, specifically because building their own version would have taken longer than adopting mine. The third team had a genuinely different latency requirement my design didn't fit, and rather than force it, I helped them identify where their needs diverged, which also sharpened the shared architecture's documented boundaries.

What I'd emphasize: the technical judgment mattered, but the actual staff-level work was making adoption cheaper than the alternative, and being honest about the one case where it didn't fit rather than forcing uniform adoption.

**Testing:** whether you can drive cross-team technical direction through voluntary adoption rather than mandate, and whether you can be honest about the limits of your own design.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Technical vision

interviewQuestions.question: Describe a situation where the org chart hadn't caught up to a real problem, and no one was formally responsible for fixing it.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Two product teams both wrote to the same core data model, with no agreed process for coordinating schema changes between them. It had caused two silent data-corruption incidents over a quarter, each traced back to one team changing a field's meaning without the other team knowing. Neither team's manager considered cross-team schema governance part of their job, and it genuinely wasn't written into anyone's role.

I didn't wait for someone to assign this. I documented both incidents with their actual cost — one required a multi-day manual data reconciliation — and proposed a lightweight governance process: any schema change touching shared fields requires a short async review from the other team before merging, with a clear two-day SLA so it wouldn't become a bottleneck.

Getting both team leads to agree took more relationship work than technical work — neither had been told by their own management to prioritize this, so I had to make the case that a two-day review was cheap insurance against a repeat of a multi-day incident, using their own past incidents as the evidence. Both agreed, and I became the de facto owner of a process that, technically, isn't anyone's explicit job description a year later.

**Testing:** whether you're comfortable acting on a real problem in the gap between two org charts, without waiting for a formal mandate that may never come.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Organizational ambiguity

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about someone you've mentored, and how you know it actually worked.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I worked with an engineer over about eight months who was strong technically but mostly executed well-scoped tickets handed to them. I deliberately shifted what I handed them: first a small ambiguous bug with no clear repro steps, then a small feature with an intentionally underspecified brief, reviewing their approach to the ambiguity itself in our 1:1s, not just the code they eventually wrote.

The evidence I'd point to that it actually worked, rather than just feeling like it did: within the year, they proposed and led a cross-team initiative on their own — something they hadn't previously had the confidence or scope-reading ability to do — and were promoted to senior partly on the strength of that initiative. I still check in with them roughly monthly, but they no longer need it for day-to-day decisions, which is itself a sign the growth held rather than being dependent on my continued involvement.

I'd distinguish this from just being a friendly, approachable presence on the team, which is valuable but isn't the same thing — the deliberate, escalating exposure to ambiguity, and a specific before/after in their independent judgment, is what makes this a demonstrable body of work rather than a vibe.

**Testing:** whether you can back a mentorship claim with specific evidence of growth and independence, rather than a vague, unfalsifiable self-description.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Mentorship

interviewQuestions.question: How do you personally distinguish between a story that's genuinely staff-scoped and one that's just a very good senior-IC story?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I use one test on every story before I use it for a staff-level prompt: if I removed myself from the story, would anyone else's work, growth, or decisions look meaningfully different? If the honest answer is no — the outcome is entirely a function of my own hours and skill — I treat it as a strong senior-IC story, which is still valuable material, just not an answer to a staff-scoped prompt.

An example that failed this test for me: I once rebuilt a recommendation engine largely alone and made it three times faster. Genuinely hard, well-executed work — but no other engineer's approach changed because of it, nothing spread past that one system, and there was no real organizational ambiguity to navigate. It's an excellent senior story. It isn't a staff story, and I don't try to dress it up as one.

A story that passed the test: the contract-testing framework I built, which twelve teams eventually adopted, ten of them without my direct involvement. Removing me from that story clearly changes the outcome for people I never worked with directly.

What I try to avoid is inventing a mentorship or multiplier angle on a story that doesn't actually have one — an interviewer's follow-up questions expose that quickly, and it's worse than honestly presenting a strong senior-scoped story as exactly that.

**Testing:** whether you have real self-awareness about the level your own material demonstrates, rather than inflating every story to sound staff-sized.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Self-calibration
